cards.q: What does IPsec provide and what are its two phases?
cards.a: IPsec provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication for IP traffic at the packet level. Its two phases are IKE (key management, UDP 500/4500) and ESP/AH (data plane).

cards.q: What is the difference between AH and ESP?
cards.a: AH (protocol 51) provides integrity and authentication but does not encrypt and has no NAT traversal; ESP (protocol 50) provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication and is the standard choice for real encryption. AH is legacy.

cards.q: What is the difference between transport mode and tunnel mode in IPsec?
cards.a: Transport mode protects only the payload and keeps the original IP header visible, used for host-to-host or GRE; tunnel mode wraps the entire IP packet in a new outer header, used for site-to-site VPNs.

cards.q: What is the purpose of IKE phases 1 and 2?
cards.a: Phase 1 authenticates the peers and builds a secure channel, producing an ISAKMP SA (main or aggressive mode). Phase 2 negotiates data-plane keys and produces the IPsec SA (quick mode).

cards.q: What ports does IKE use, and when is each used?
cards.a: ISAKMP uses UDP 500; NAT-T wraps ESP in UDP 4500 when NAT is between the peers. NAT-T is used to allow ESP to pass through NAT.

cards.q: What is the difference between main mode and aggressive mode in IKE?
cards.a: Main mode uses 6 messages and is secure; aggressive mode uses 3 messages and is faster but weaker.

cards.q: What are the differences between IKEv1 and IKEv2?
cards.a: IKEv1 has two phases (1+2) with complex SA negotiation and legacy status; IKEv2 uses one exchange with simpler SA negotiation, native/built-in NAT-T, and is the preferred modern standard.

cards.q: What does an IPsec transform-set pair together?
cards.a: A transform-set pairs an encryption algorithm (esp-aes) with an integrity algorithm (esp-sha-hmac), defining both encryption and integrity for the tunnel.

cards.q: How is the crypto map attached in legacy IPsec configuration?
cards.a: The crypto map (for example crypto map CM 10 ipsec-isakmp) is attached to the physical interface with the crypto map command, and it defines the peer, transform-set, and the interesting-traffic ACL via match address.

cards.q: What is the modern approach to IPsec configuration used by DMVPN and FlexVPN?
cards.a: The modern approach uses an IKEv2 profile plus an IPsec profile instead of the legacy crypto map and ISAKMP configuration, simplifying configuration.

cards.q: Which commands verify IPsec SA and IKE state?
cards.a: show crypto isakmp sa, show crypto ipsec sa, show crypto map, show crypto session, debug crypto isakmp, and debug crypto ipsec.

cards.q: Tunnel is up but no traffic passes through IPsec; what is a likely cause?
cards.a: A crypto map ACL mismatch in the match address statement means the interesting traffic doesn't match, so no IPsec SA is created. Check the match address ACL.

cards.q: What happens when NAT breaks ESP, and how is it fixed?
cards.a: NAT can break ESP; NAT-T wraps ESP in UDP 4500 to allow it through NAT between the peers.

cards.q: What causes a transform-set mismatch between IPsec peers?
cards.a: The peers have different algorithms configured in their transform-sets; both ends must use the same encryption and integrity algorithms, such as esp-aes with esp-sha-hmac.

cards.q: What is the IPsec quick-review summary?
cards.a: ESP encrypts, AH authenticates only, tunnel mode wraps the entire packet, transport protects only the payload, IKE uses UDP 500, NAT-T uses UDP 4500, phase 1 produces the ISAKMP SA, phase 2 produces the IPsec SA, and the transform is esp-aes plus esp-sha.
